overview: An Elastic Network Interface (ENI) is the logical VPC component that represents a virtual network card attached to an EC2 instance. The exam tests what an ENI can carry (IP addresses, Elastic IPs, security groups, a MAC address) and the two structural rules that drive scenario answers: an ENI is bound to a single Availability Zone, yet it can be detached and moved to another instance. That combination is the classic low-cost failover pattern, so expect questions where moving an ENI is the right answer only if the target instance sits in the same AZ.

coreConcepts.definition: A logical component in a VPC that represents a virtual network card; it is the network identity an EC2 instance uses to reach the VPC.
An ENI can have a primary private IPv4, one or more secondary IPv4 addresses, one Elastic IP (IPv4) per private IPv4, one public IPv4, one or more security groups, and a MAC address.
The main private IPv4 address of the ENI; every ENI has one primary private IPv4 address.
Additional private IPv4 addresses that an ENI can carry alongside the primary one (one or more).
Each private IPv4 on the ENI can be associated with one Elastic IP; the pairing rule is one Elastic IP per private IPv4.
The ENI can have one public IPv4 address, separate from any Elastic IP association.
One or more security groups can be attached to an ENI, making the ENI the point where security-group rules apply to that network interface.
Each ENI has its own MAC address, which travels with the ENI when it is moved between instances.
The network interface an instance is created with, shown as Eth0 in the example; it carries the instance's primary private IP (for example 192.168.0.31).
An additional interface attached to an instance, shown as Eth1 with its own private IP (for example 192.168.0.42); this is the type typically detached and re-attached for failover.
An ENI can be created independently of an instance and attached or moved to EC2 instances while running, which enables failover.
An ENI is bound to one specific Availability Zone; it can only be attached to instances in that same AZ.

mustRemember: An ENI is bound to a specific Availability Zone — it cannot be attached to an instance in a different AZ.
An ENI can be created independently of an instance and attached/moved onto instances on the fly.
An ENI has exactly one primary private IPv4 and can have one or more secondary private IPv4 addresses.
The Elastic IP rule is one Elastic IP (IPv4) per private IPv4 address on the ENI.
An ENI can have one public IPv4 address.
An ENI can have one or more security groups, and it has a MAC address.
Moving an ENI to another instance carries its private IPs, Elastic IPs, security groups and MAC address with it.

keyComparisons.items: Primary private IPv4 vs secondary private IPv4
keyComparisons.difference: Every ENI has one primary private IPv4; secondaries are optional and can be one or more, and each private IPv4 can pair with one Elastic IP.

keyComparisons.items: Elastic IP vs public IPv4 on an ENI
keyComparisons.difference: An Elastic IP is associated per private IPv4, while the ENI has a single public IPv4 attribute.

keyComparisons.items: ENI in one AZ vs ENI across AZs
keyComparisons.difference: An ENI lives in exactly one AZ, so failover by moving an ENI only works to an instance in the same AZ.
Eth0 is the instance's original interface carrying the primary private IP; the secondary ENI is the separately created interface that can be moved for failover.

keyComparisons.items: Moving an ENI vs re-creating an instance
keyComparisons.difference: Moving the ENI preserves the network identity (private IP, Elastic IP, MAC, security groups), whereas a new instance in another AZ cannot take that ENI.

commonMisunderstandings: An ENI can be moved between any instances — wrong: only to instances in the same Availability Zone, because the ENI is AZ-bound.
An ENI can have several Elastic IPs per single private IPv4 — wrong: it is one Elastic IP per private IPv4.
Secondary IP addresses are attached to the instance rather than the ENI — wrong: private IPv4 addresses, including secondaries, belong to the ENI.
Security groups are properties of the EC2 instance only — security groups are attached to the ENI, and the ENI carries them when moved.
You must terminate an instance to change its networking identity — an independently created ENI can be attached on the fly.
A public IPv4 and an Elastic IP are the same attribute — the ENI's listed attributes treat one public IPv4 and Elastic-IP-per-private-IPv4 separately.
mentalModels: Think of an ENI as a physical network card you can unplug from one server and plug into another in the same rack (AZ) — the MAC, IPs and security settings go with the card.
Think of the AZ binding as the ENI being welded to one data center: moving it to another AZ is physically impossible.
Think of private IPv4 addresses as slots on the card, each slot able to hold one Elastic IP.
edgeCases: The failover move is only valid when the replacement instance is in the same AZ as the ENI.
Moving a secondary ENI onto a different instance preserves the addresses and MAC, so clients using that address see continuity.
The instance's own Eth0 stays with the original instance; the movable unit is the separately created ENI (for example Eth1).

whenToUse.situation: A running instance fails and you need its private/Elastic IP and MAC to follow a standby instance quickly without changing DNS or client config
whenToUse.use: Detach the secondary ENI from the failed instance and attach it to the standby instance in the same AZ.

whenToUse.situation: You need an interface that exists independently of any instance and can be attached later
whenToUse.use: Create the ENI independently, then attach it on the fly.

whenToUse.situation: The standby instance is in a different Availability Zone
whenToUse.use: Moving the ENI does not work — the ENI is bound to its AZ, so failover by ENI is constrained to the same AZ.

patternsToRecognize.signal: 'Preserve private IP / MAC / security groups when an instance is replaced'
patternsToRecognize.indicates: Moving an Elastic Network Interface to the replacement instance.

patternsToRecognize.signal: 'Attach network interface on the fly' or 'move network interface'
patternsToRecognize.indicates: ENI detach/attach failover pattern, valid only within the same AZ.

examTraps.trap: Option: move the ENI to an instance in another Availability Zone for cross-AZ failover
examTraps.correction: The ENI is bound to a specific AZ; it can only be attached to instances in that AZ.

examTraps.trap: Option: attach multiple Elastic IPs to one private IPv4
examTraps.correction: The rule is one Elastic IP (IPv4) per private IPv4.

examTraps.trap: Option: give the ENI multiple public IPv4 addresses
examTraps.correction: The ENI has one public IPv4.

examTraps.trap: Option: ENI is a subnet-level or Region-level construct
examTraps.correction: The ENI is a logical VPC component bound to one Availability Zone.

examTraps.trap: Option: security groups are configured on the instance and lost if you swap interfaces
examTraps.correction: The ENI carries one or more security groups and keeps them when moved.

beyondSource: (Tutor knowledge) AWS also supports per-ENI IPv6 addresses and multiple ENIs per instance, but the source's testable attributes here are the IPv4 ones, Elastic IPs, one public IPv4, security groups and MAC.
(Tutor knowledge) Elastic IPs are associated with the private IPv4, so moving the ENI moves the Elastic IP association as well — useful for failover without DNS changes.
